clue.text: Latin-American flower of variegated petal

indicators.note: variegated means of mixed colours, so the letters of petal are mixed up

explanation.surface: A South American bloom with multicoloured petals.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flower' is something that flows, a river: the River Plate (Río de la Plata) lies between Argentina and Uruguay. 'variegated' rearranges PETAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The River Plate is the great South American estuary, and a river is a thing that flows.

clue.text: Voltaire's novel doctor with the polish of a Greek god

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of shepherds and woodland
a polish or shine is a gloss

explanation.surface: Voltaire's fictional physician has the sheen of a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: The doctor is Dr Pangloss, the relentless optimist tutor in Voltaire's novel Candide.
explanation.definitionFit: The ever-hopeful tutor in Candide is called Dr Pangloss, a doctor of philosophy in Voltaire's story.

clue.text: It is in a toga of sorts, not notably shaken

indicators.note: in says one piece goes inside the other
a toga of sorts is a rearranged version of the words a toga

explanation.surface: Someone wrapped in a makeshift toga, yet visibly rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of sorts' rearranges A TOGA to AGATO, and 'in' puts IT inside it. The printed 'not' reads as 'but', a one-letter misread. 'notably' hints at musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: In a musical score the Italian marking means to be played in an agitated, restless manner.

clue.text: Poet's satisfying want

parts.note: what satisfies a want is a sufficient amount, given here in the archaic form a poet would use

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' signals an old or literary word; the word is the archaic form of 'enough', which is what satisfies a want.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic poetic word means sufficient, the quantity that meets a need.

clue.text: Goes for the financial gain

definitions.meaning: the money taken from a sale or event

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means advances or moves on; as a plural noun it means the takings or profit from a sale.

clue.text: He came suddenly on Friday

parts.note: Defoe's castaway came upon his companion, the man he named Friday after the day they met

explanation.walkthrough: 'on Friday' looks like a day of the week, but Friday is the castaway's servant in Defoe's novel, whom he came upon unexpectedly. The printed 'Le' is a misread 'He'.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's shipwrecked hero discovers the islander Friday and makes him his servant.

clue.text: Having the effrontery to be unfriendly

explanation.surface: Someone has the cheek to be standoffish.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both calm audacity and a frosty, distant manner.

clue.text: Supposedly a bad outlook for someone …

definitions.text: Supposedly a bad outlook for someone …

parts.words: Supposedly a bad outlook for someone …
parts.note: a look believed to bring harm to whoever receives it, so a bad outlook for them

explanation.walkthrough: 'outlook' reads as prospects, but it is a literal look outward: the malicious gaze that superstition says brings misfortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore holds that a malevolent glance can curse its target with bad luck.

clue.text: … who may be an object of ridicule

definitions.text: … who may be an object of ridicule

parts.words: … who may be an object of ridicule
parts.note: the person on the receiving end of a look, and also someone who looks ridiculous, as in 'you look a fright'

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 7 down: the person looked at is in sight, and someone absurd-looking is said to 'look a sight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying someone looks a sight means they look laughable or a mess.

clue.text: Satan's offer to snobs? Certainly a fast one

definitions.text: Satan's offer to snobs? Certainly a fast one

parts.words: Satan's offer to snobs? Certainly a fast one
parts.note: the devil's underworld trading hides to shoemakers, and a phrase meaning at breakneck speed

explanation.walkthrough: A 'snob' is an old British word for a cobbler, who would want hide; the fast one is the speed, not a trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means recklessly fast, originally of galloping riders.

clue.text: First thing some find in to health

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'First thing some find in to health', is garbled: NO 1 (first thing) + SOME is clear, but 'find in to health' gives no definition (perhaps 'injurious to health' misread) and no scan or search gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: First thing some find in to health

clue.text: Roaring to success?

parts.note: making a loud deep noise, and also thriving, as a business does in good times

explanation.walkthrough: 'Roaring' is both a loud noise and, as in 'a roaring trade', flourishing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both resonantly loud and enjoying rapid growth or prosperity.

clue.text: Artistic writer who made nonsense of 22 across

indicators.note: making nonsense of a word jumbles its letters into a new order

parts.note: this points back to the first word of the 22 across entry

explanation.surface: A painter-poet who wrote absurd verse about another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear was a painter as well as the author of nonsense verse, so 'made nonsense of' is both the anagram signal and a nod to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear was a Victorian landscape painter and illustrator famous for his limericks and nonsense poems.

clue.text: Bit of fun in a Scottish dance

definitions.meaning: a brief spell of carefree enjoyment or a short affair

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a short indulgent episode, and the Highland version is a lively solo Scottish dance.

clue.text: Pets can be such a nuisance

indicators.note: can be suggests the letters may become something else when rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges PETS.
explanation.definitionFit: An annoying person or creature is a bother or irritant.

clue.text: Berlin banker's merry frolic

definitions.meaning: the river with banks that runs through Berlin; the 's reads as 'is'
a bout of carefree, excessive fun

explanation.walkthrough: A 'banker' here is a thing with banks, a river: the Spree flows through Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spree is the river of Berlin, and a bout of indulgence such as a shopping binge shares its name.

clue.text: Brave woman

parts.note: the wife of a Native American warrior, a 'brave', rather than a courageous woman

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' is a noun for a Native American warrior. The answer is an old term now regarded as offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: The dated word denoted a Native American woman or wife, the partner of a warrior.

clue.text: Emulate Kate Hardcastle bent on winning

definitions.meaning: copy the heroine of Goldsmith's comedy, who poses as a barmaid to win Marlow
bend low in order to triumph

explanation.surface: A theatre fan copies a heroine, determined to come out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate Hardcastle is the heroine of Oliver Goldsmith's 1773 comedy, whose title gives the phrase. 'bent on' reads as 'determined', but is 'bow down in order to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldsmith's heroine lowers herself to a servant's role to win her suitor, which is to bow down so as to triumph.

clue.text: Fragile container

parts.note: a brittle natural casing that holds a yolk and white

explanation.definitionFit: The thin calcium casing of a hen's laying is proverbially delicate.

clue.text: Pace English set in a form of sport

indicators.note: put in a new form, these words are reshaped into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: An English gait set into some athletic pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a form of' rearranges PACE, ENGLISH and SET together.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing horses or runners over fences and ditches is a recognised sporting event.

clue.text: Browned-off by having one's health drunk

definitions.meaning: browned under a grill, playing on the slang for fed up
having glasses raised in one's honour

explanation.surface: Someone fed up despite everyone drinking to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browned-off' is British slang for fed up; here it means crisped under heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread browned under heat has the same name as a person honoured with raised glasses.

clue.text: Type inclined to be emphatic

parts.note: sloping print used to stress words, rather than a person given to emphasis

explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' reads as a kind of person, but it is printing type, slanted ('inclined') and used for emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: Slanted lettering is the usual way of stressing a word in print.

clue.text: A revue all variety, for what it's worth

indicators.note: a variety show mixes acts, so the letters are mixed up too

explanation.surface: A revue made entirely of variety acts, judged on its merits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges A REVUE ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The true worth of something, adjusted for inflation, is what an economist calls its actual worth.

clue.text: Clergyman doesn't finish on the right page of the book

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a rector is a parish clergyman

explanation.surface: A vicar stops halfway through reading the correct page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't finish' drops the last letter of RECTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing, the right-hand page of an open book is given this Latin name.

clue.text: See 22
Songs that make a ben productive?

definitions.meaning: what a hen does when it produces eggs

explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'ben' is a misread 'hen'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means ballads, and also what a hen does with eggs.

clue.text: Familiar handwriting

parts.note: an informal word for a person's handwriting, also a clenched hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar' means colloquial: the slang word for handwriting is also a clenched hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially a person's script is named after the hand that writes it.

clue.text: Impounded member

parts.note: split as 'Im pounded', IM placed within LB, the abbreviation for pound, gives a body part

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Impounded' as 'IM pounded': IM inside LB (pound). The word cannot be split for the parse, so it stands as one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm or leg is a member of the body.

clue.text: Tom's favourite food, maybe

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, and fish is a cat's favourite, so a fish named after the animal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name, but is a tomcat.
explanation.definitionFit: The whiskered freshwater fish is named after a feline.

clue.text: Put a protective coat round cooking dixies

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O

indicators.note: cooking means mixing up, so the letters of dixies are stirred

explanation.surface: Applying a protective layer around some army cooking pots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' rearranges DIXIES; a dixie is a large army cooking pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Coating a metal with a layer formed by reaction with air protects it from further corrosion.

clue.text: Same excuse told once again?

parts.note: a familiar, often-repeated explanation, a tale heard many times before

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a stale, familiar excuse or situation.

clue.text: Seasoned Birkenhead sailmaker

parts.note: the head of Birken is B, and sail made over gives the rest; the whole names a culinary herb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Birkenhead' is a town on the Mersey, but its head is B; 'maker' remakes SAIL. The herb seasons food.
explanation.definitionFit: The aromatic herb is used to season dishes.
